claims.text: A 1–2 µm Al2O3 coating applied to boride-based components will significantly improve resistance to corrosion by molten aluminum.
The Al2O3 coating can be deposited by CVD at 600–700 °C using an adhesion-promoting interlayer.
The proposed deposition is performed in a low-pressure controlled environment.
Temperatures of 660–750 °C represent relevant molten-aluminum exposure conditions for hot-dip aluminum-plating cycles.
CVD deposition with an adhesion-promoting interlayer will produce a dense, uniform, adherent Al2O3 layer.
The Al2O3 layer will remain intact under high-temperature plating conditions.
Compact alumina layers can act as diffusion barriers that inhibit corrosive transport.
Al2O3 is chemically inert and stable in direct contact with molten aluminum at 660–750 °C.
The Al2O3 layer prevents molten aluminum from directly contacting the boride substrate.
The Al2O3 layer prevents molten aluminum from reacting with and penetrating into the boride substrate.
Preventing molten-aluminum reaction and penetration will reduce interfacial degradation and corrosion.
Coated boride substrates will have a lower corrosion-penetration rate than uncoated boride substrates during molten-aluminum exposure.
Coated boride substrates will undergo less overall material degradation and weight loss than uncoated controls.
Uncoated boride-based components typically undergo rapid degradation and deep corrosion penetration in molten aluminum.
Protection will persist only while the coating remains continuous and adherent.
Cracking or delamination caused by repeated thermal cycling or mechanical stress will diminish the coating's protective performance.
Long-term durability under cyclic thermal and mechanical stress is undetermined.
The adhesion-layer parameters have not yet been precisely optimized.

contradictions.description: The adhesion layer is repeatedly described as optimized, while the uncertainty field states that its parameters remain to be optimized; no optimization procedure or fixed formulation is supplied.
